title: Gross National Happiness Concept Introduced
reason: Multiple independent, non-Wikipedia sources confirm King Jigme Singye Wangchuck of Bhutan originated the Gross National Happiness (GNH) concept — the idea that national progress should be measured by collective wellbeing rather than GDP alone. The exact year the king first articulated this is genuinely disputed across sources (some cite 1972, tied to his ascension to the throne; some cite a documented 1979 Bombay-airport interview with Indian journalists returning from the Havana NAM summit as the moment the phrase became internationally known), but the Asian Development Bank's feature 'Gross National Happiness in Bhutan: 12 Things to Know' (adb.org) explicitly states GNH was 'first introduced' by the king 'during the mid-1970s' — directly consistent with the event's hedged 'around 1976' framing. The core substance (GNH as GDP alternative measuring wellbeing) and country/actor are corroborated by many additional independent sources (Asahi Glass Foundation/Blue Planet Prize, GNH Centre Bhutan, JSW Law School Bhutan, OPHI) even though they disagree amongst themselves on the precise year (ranging 1972-1979), which is itself evidence the 'around 1976' hedge in the description is a defensible position within scholarly disagreement rather than a clear error. The four-pillars framework (sustainable development, environment, culture, governance) is the well-documented, widely-cited structure of GNH as it came to be applied, though it was more formally operationalized later (Centre for Bhutan Studies, est. 1998) — a timing nuance common to almost all general descriptions of GNH's history and not treated as a material misstatement of actor/country/core event.

title: Third Repatriation Pilot Programme Collapses
reason: The substance is real but the year is wrong. The joint Bhutan-Nepal Joint Verification Team (JVT) screened the one pilot camp (Khudunabari, ~12,600 people) in the field between March-December 2001, but withheld results until June 2003. The four-category classification (bona fide citizens, voluntary emigrants, non-Bhutanese, criminals) was confirmed and the restrictive repatriation terms (only the 2.4% in Category 1 eligible) were locked in during the 15th round of bilateral talks in October 2003, after which HRW states 'no progress has been made' and no Khudunabari residents were ever repatriated. This is the collapse described in the event: a joint committee finishing camp assessment, identifying return categories, and Bhutan refusing citizenship to the majority, causing the process to stall. All of that concluded in 2003, not 2007. By 2007 the pivot to third-country resettlement (the Core Group of 8 nations) was already underway as a consequence of the multi-year-old collapse, not concurrent with it. So country and substance check out, but the year is off by about four years.

title: Nepal Earthquake Causes Damage in Southern Bhutan
reason: The April 25, 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal was indeed felt in Bhutan, but multiple independent sources contradict the specific claims in the event description. First, geography: sources consistently place the felt tremors in western Bhutan (Thimphu registered Mercalli intensity IV), not "southern and eastern Bhutan" as claimed. Second and more importantly, substance: contemporaneous reporting states Bhutanese officials reported "no reports of any damage or loss to property" and a Bhutanese minister said "Everything is fine in Bhutan" — directly contradicting the claim of infrastructure damage and casualties in Bhutan. One Kuensel (Bhutan's national paper) reference mentions minor building cracks in Thimphu, but this is cosmetic and in the wrong region, not the "damaging infrastructure and causing casualties" described. No source found for landslides occurring in Bhutan from this event, nor for any resulting Bhutanese building-code enforcement changes — Bhutan's response was instead sending a 63-person medical team and a Nu. 62 million relief fund to Nepal, i.e., Bhutan was a donor/helper, not a damage site. The core disaster-impact claims in the event (landslides, infrastructure damage, casualties, building-code reform) are unsupported and actively contradicted by every source found; only the trivially-true fact that tremors were felt in Bhutan holds up.
